summary: This informational RFC introduces VRRP-aware PIM, a way for PIM to track Virtual Router Redundancy Protocol state and keep multicast traffic flowing on failover. The mechanism is based on a Cisco IOS implementation.

plainLanguage.summary: When a backup router takes over, the multicast system follows along so video keeps flowing.

questions: how does pim failover with vrrp
what is a pim designated router
subtitle: Keeping multicast flowing when routers fail over

tldr.problem: VRRP handles failover for unicast traffic by switching to a backup router, but PIM multicast routing operates independently and may send traffic through the wrong router after a VRRP failover, causing duplicate traffic or interruptions.
tldr.mechanism: VRRP-aware PIM makes PIM listen to VRRP state changes, automatically adjusting the Designated Router priority so the VRRP Master Router becomes the PIM DR and can properly forward multicast Join/Prune messages after failover.
tldr.outcome: Multicast traffic is consistently forwarded through the active VRRP router without duplication or loss, allowing both unicast and multicast redundancy to work in concert.

today: RFC 7910 is an Informational RFC and has not been obsoleted. It describes a vendor-specific implementation technique documented for interoperability purposes, remaining a reference for network operators implementing redundant multicast routing with VRRP or HSRP.

sections.title: The Multicast Failover Problem
sections.content:
The Virtual Router Redundancy Protocol (VRRP) provides redundancy by maintaining a virtual IP address shared by multiple routers. One router is elected the Master Router, which owns the virtual IP and forwards traffic. If the Master fails, another router takes over, automatically and transparently to end hosts.

The Protocol Independent Multicast (PIM) system routes multicast traffic from source to multiple receivers. PIM elects a Designated Router on each LAN segment to forward Join/Prune messages toward the Rendezvous Point. However, PIM has no awareness of VRRP state. When VRRP fails over to a backup router, PIM may still route through the old router, causing duplicate multicast traffic (two routers forwarding the same stream) or interruptions.

VRRP-aware PIM solves this by making PIM listen to VRRP state changes and automatically adjusting its Designated Router election to ensure the VRRP Master Router also becomes the multicast Designated Router.
sections.plainLanguage: When a backup router takes over, it becomes the main router for both regular and multicast traffic, so everything flows through the same place.

sections.title: Tracking State and Adjusting Priority
sections.content:
VRRP-aware PIM works by having each router's PIM component subscribe to state-change notifications from VRRP. When a router becomes the VRRP Master Router, PIM automatically applies a high Designated Router priority value to ensure that router wins the DR election.

Upon failover, PIM sends an additional Hello message using the VRRP virtual IP as the source address. This Hello contains a new Generation Identifier (GenID), which signals to other routers that a neighbor has changed. Downstream routers respond by immediately sending triggered Join/Prune messages toward the virtual IP address. Upstream routers process these J/P messages and create multicast routing states on the new Master Router, directing traffic through it.

The RFC also notes an alternative implementation where passive routers maintain multicast route state and remember the Master Router's GenID, allowing the new Master to reuse existing state rather than resending Join/Prune messages.
sections.plainLanguage: PIM watches VRRP and gives high priority to whichever router VRRP picks as the main one. When failover happens, PIM sends a hello message to tell everyone a change happened, so downstream routers send their subscription requests to the new main router.

sections.title: Handling Duplicates and Multiple VRRP Groups
sections.content:
After a VRRP failover, the old Master Router may still be forwarding multicast traffic momentarily, creating duplicates. PIM Assert handles this: routers that receive multicast on multiple interfaces compare metrics to determine which should forward. In VRRP-aware PIM, passive routers send a high penalty metric (PIM_ASSERT_INFINITY minus 1) to let the Master Router win the Assert election and stop sending.

The same mechanism applies to Designated Forwarder election in bidirectional PIM groups: passive VRRP routers send a penalty metric in DF offers to ensure the Master Router wins DF election.

If multiple VRRP groups are configured on an interface, the adjustment only takes effect if all groups are in passive state. This allows load balancing: if at least one VRRP group is active on a router, that router may win DR or Assert elections using its normal metric, enabling both active groups to participate in multicast routing.
sections.plainLanguage: If the old router is still sending copies of the stream, PIM has routers say stop, and let someone else take over. If multiple backup groups are set up, this only applies when all are waiting, so active groups can still handle traffic.

sections.title: Deployment and Compatibility
sections.content:
VRRP-aware PIM can be safely deployed selectively. Routers that do not support this feature will not break functionality, provided their DR priority does not conflict with participating routers. When deployed in a network with dynamic routing, downstream routers should configure static routes with the VRRP virtual IP as the next-hop address for PIM Join/Prune messages in order to benefit from this mechanism.

The feature works with any redundancy protocol that can provide state-change notifications to the multicast routing system. While designed for VRRP, the same scheme can enable HSRP-aware PIM with similar failover and tracking mechanisms, as HSRP provides similar redundancy functions despite differences in timer intervals and the number of backup routers.

This mechanism requires no changes to the PIM or VRRP message formats, making it transparent and backward-compatible with existing implementations.
sections.plainLanguage: Other routers do not need to know about this feature; it works quietly and does not break anything. It can work with other failover systems too, like HSRP. No new message types are needed.
